newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Reading between Costello's monetary lines.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Reading between Costello's monetary lines.

text.p: Australian Treasurer Peter Costello is being very careful not to usurp the Reserve Bank's monetary authority, but he is nonetheless delivering a very bullish message about interest rates.
The message has to be read between the lines, but it is pretty unambiguous.
Prime Minister John Howard earlier gave a very strong hint that satisfactory wage data might prompt a rate cut, so reporters badgered Costello five times on the subject at his 0200 GMT appearance.
Reporter: "Is it time for interest rates to come down?"

Costello: "We've always made it entirely clear that the Reserve will take the decision in relation to interest rates. But we've had a target for inflation -- two to three percent underlying inflation. We're bang in the middle of the target.
"We've said that in order to get that target, you'd want to see wages below four percent. Today's quarterly survey is consistent with that.
"So you've got indicators that are showing that it is all coming together and they're showing that we are taking the steps that are required to make sure we have a good monetary policy."

This reporter thought he was just dodging, although the answer did seem deliberately bullish. But Costello kept saying similar bullish things every time he was asked about interest rates, suggesting that he was trying to go as close as he could to saying a cut was on the cards.
In the second monetary-policy question he was asked about Howard's monetary comment. He responded first by repeating that it was up to the bank, looking at conditions a year away, and then added:
"But as I said earlier -- two days, two good-news results. It's coming together. Low inflation. Good growth prospects." (And then he pointed to the narrowing U.S.-Australian bond margin.)
For the third attempt, a reporter asked whether Australians would get some kind of reward by Christmas.

Costello: "As a general principle I point out that low inflation and moderate wage growth always brings its own rewards and the rewards that it brings is it lessens pressure in relation to interest rates. But what the levels are at any particular time will be determined by the Reserve Bank."
In attempt number four another reporter asked whether there was any reason why monetary policy should not now be eased.

Costello: "Well I keep making the point that the right economic indicators always point to good economic outcomes and low inflation, moderate wage growth, the right economic indicators, two days, two good-news stories, and that will over time always bring its own rewards.
"But I'm not going to speculate on the particular amounts or the particular decisions which may be taken by the Reserve."
Reporter: "Do the results actually put downward pressure on rates?"

Costello: "Well, let me put it this way: Low inflation, moderate wage growth will always relieve pressure in relation to interest rates, but you can't take from that what the level is going to be at any particular time."
Apart from a perfunctory reference to the Reserve Bank having to watch out for conditions a year away, Costello made no comment bearish for interest rates.
His message is clear.
-- Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
